textPlacement.assessment: Pass for this exact 18–24-month placement. The title names the new-baby situation despite its gentle “Room for” opening. The row itself preserves difficult feelings and immediate adult protection. Detail makes helping optional, accepts available extra hands, and offers ordinary books, toys, errands and time together without a daily quota or an expectation that the toddler will love the baby. It does not promote prenatal preparations, an infant-handling setup, a fixed motive, or a big-sibling duty. The displayed broad toddler context is a browsing aid, with no starting-age expectation.

Pass. The recognizable shared-problem title and topic row pair neutral support with stopping harm and enough adult help. Detail allows actions as preverbal participation, adults supplying most solutions, proportional presence and separation before problem solving. It neither makes neutrality a requirement to watch violence nor turns the six source alternatives into a checklist. Individual needs can differ and sibling friendship is not required. The text avoids both a creative-solution guarantee and a demand for identical parental time.

Pass. The title recognizes both the child using the object and the child waiting. Crucially, the topic row already names the home/public-place distinction; a reader need not open detail to discover the courtesy exception. Full text includes adult help, stopping physical conflict, noticing whether company is welcome, and child input before visitors. The displayed parallel-play age is attributed to Davies and explicitly allows experience variation without a sharing deadline. No universal countdown, unlimited public turn, or independent dispute-solving requirement is created.

Pass. The title describes watching before joining and the row offers proximity and support without treating quieter temperament as a defect. Preparation, a tour, a greeting or stop phrase, and an early or shorter visit are concrete possibilities with adult availability. The language avoids a guaranteed eventual departure from the parent, a fixed shy label, comparison with outgoing peers, and prescribed social performance. The 18–24-month placement does not turn these examples into speech or sociability milestones.

Pass. The short row preserves offered affection, noticing welcome and the adult’s protective responsibility. Full text explains a pulling-away child and supports the enthusiastic child without shaming either. Ordinary touch and elective help are distinguished from necessary gentle care and immediate protection, using the cited limits context. The natural invitation to offer affection is appropriate; it need not become an impersonal care disclaimer or a new consent procedure.

Pass. The title and row offer something an adult can actually say or notice, while explicitly preserving delight. Detail distinguishes describing an action from fixing a child’s identity and allows waiting during concentration; it does not require silence, emotional restraint, constant narration, or a ban on every descriptive action word. The private disposition appropriately avoids promoting categorical praise outcomes and mutual sibling supervision. The few “room” phrases here remain tied to concrete examples rather than substituting for useful guidance.

issues.surface: 18-24 play-discovery and connection-feelings topic-row headings; detail heading
issues.finding: “The experiences Davies wants to leave room for” does not identify screens or a recognizable screen-related family situation. In the inspected title-only topic context it joins several “room” formulations and could describe almost any activity. The summary supplies the missing subject, but the heading itself is the main scanning cue.
issues.requiredCorrection: Replace this heading with a short title that explicitly identifies screens and the attributed perspective, for example a title about Davies’s approach to screens. Preserve the qualified summary and anecdote treatment; do not replace the title with an imperative screen rule.

issues.surface: Detail: Back to the books, Screen time reference
issues.finding: The rendered phrase “complete personal-experience continuation” describes an editor’s reading obligation rather than helping a parent locate the book discussion. HomeStudy.jsx renders this locator verbatim, so it is public copy.
issues.requiredCorrection: Replace the locator with plain book-navigation wording naming screen alternatives, adult example and Davies’s family experience. Keep the completion/continuation verification in private evidence or review records and retain the exact PDF span.

textPlacement.assessment: Revise two narrow public fields. In both topic contexts, the summary and full prose are otherwise proportionate: Davies’s firsthand-experience preference, adult modeling and feasible alternatives are attributed; occasional programs and later computer skills remain family experience rather than a zero-screen rule or developmental promise. There is no minute quota or new distress protocol. The abstract title makes retrieval harder, and the first reference locator visibly exposes review-process language. These findings do not call for excluding the topic or rewriting its qualified body.

issues.surface: Detail: Back to the books, Bilingualism reference
issues.finding: The locator ends with “surrounding asserted outcomes.” That is an editorial judgment about claims deliberately held in private provenance; it does not identify a recognizable section for the reader and makes the reference sound like a review note.
issues.requiredCorrection: Use a plain locator such as the two named language approaches and the multilingual-family example. Keep the assessments and held developmental assertions in private provenance; retain the exact PDF pages and the body’s distinction between an example and a fluency timetable.

textPlacement.assessment: Revise the public reference locator only. Both topic rows and full prose offer recognizable multilingual-family arrangements, preserve people-based and setting-based approaches as alternatives, and avoid time quotas, vocabulary milestones, effortless fluency, a universal no-delay reassurance or a mother-tongue prerequisite. The anecdote remains illustrative rather than a promised outcome. The body is useful and restrained; the open issue concerns private evaluative language displayed under Back to the books.

learnings.observation: The frozen HomeStudy reference renderer exposes locator strings verbatim. In this batch, continuation/completeness language and evaluations of held outcomes therefore appear as parent-facing reference copy even though the main body has already handled the source qualifications carefully.
learnings.action: Keep reader locators as plain navigational descriptions and preserve read-completeness and held-claim judgments in private provenance. Review the rendered Back to the books block whenever locators change.
